entries.title: [Editorial] Sudan: a health catastrophe ignored
entries.description: Sudan's women and children are paying the highest price for a war the world barely acknowledges. 12 million people have been displaced by conflict and more than half are children—many are malnourished, separated from their families, or traumatised. Pregnant women are forced to give birth without skilled attendants, sterile equipment, or access to emergency obstetric care. Gender-based violence is surging: reports from Amnesty International and UNICEF document the systematic use of rape as a weapon of war, including against girls aged as young as 1 year.

entries.title: [Comment] Personalising PARP inhibitor combinations for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
entries.description: Prostate cancer is a major cause of cancer-related mortality in men and the burden is forecast to increase significantly over the next decade.1 The outcome of patients diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer can be highly variable but cancers with BRCA gene alterations have worse outcomes.2 BRCA protein loss occurs in approximately 10% of advanced prostate cancers. PARP inhibition is an established treatment for patients with BRCA-mutant tumours progressing after androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs), at which time the treatments both delay progression and prolong survival.

entries.title: [Comment] Chasing the end of helminths: is elimination within reach?
entries.description: Soil-transmitted helminths are a group of parasitic intestinal worms that infect roughly 1·5 billion people globally. The most prevalent species are Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworms. WHO aims to eliminate soil-transmitted helminths as a public health problem by 2030, which is defined as reaching a less than 2% prevalence of moderate and heavy intensity infections (as detected using coprological approaches, such as the Kato–Katz method).1 The central element of controlling soil-transmitted helminths is the widespread administration of anthelmintics to at-risk populations

As Sarah Hawkes and her colleagues demonstrated, such attacks are part of a well-funded, global right-wing movement that over the past two decades has sought to challenge the concept of gender and erase it from public policy and discourse. entries.title: [Correspondence] A continental call to action to end cholera by 2030
entries.description: On June 4, 2025, the Assembly of Heads of State and Government from 20 cholera-affected countries in Africa united to adopt a collective call to action aimed at stopping ongoing cholera outbreaks and hastening efforts to eliminate cholera across the continent by 2030. This call represents an unprecedented political commitment to address cholera as a major public health issue in Africa. entries.title: [Correspondence] Impact of conflict on cholera epidemiology in Sudan
entries.description: When water and hospitals become targets of conflict, cholera becomes inevitable. Since April, 2023, Sudan has been engulfed in armed conflict that has systematically destroyed civilian infrastructure. This structural violence has transformed cholera from a controllable disease into a cause of recurrent epidemics, with three distinct waves recorded since mid-2023.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Innovation in health and humanitarian aid: lessons from Sudan
entries.description: Since civil war broke out in April, 2023, nearly half of Sudan's 50 million people now face acute food insecurity, 14·5 million people have been forcibly displaced, outbreaks of multiple infectious diseases have been reported, and thousands of women and children have experienced sexual violence.1 Delivery of essential services is insufficient, with more than 70% of health-care facilities in conflict-affected areas damaged or destroyed, and aid delivery systematically obstructed by both sides of the conflict.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Compassionate child obesity care within a stigmatising society
entries.description: The UK National Health Service Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics were established to provide holistic, person-centred care to treat obesity and related comorbidities in children and young people. Recent findings, presented at the European Congress on Obesity 2025,1 showed that nearly 5000 children have entered regional CEW services since 2021. These data highlight the characteristics of children and young people accessing the clinics, who often live in the most deprived areas, are of diverse ethnic heritage, and nearly a quarter have a learning disability or are neurodiverse.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Cadonilimab in advanced cervical cancer: the COMPASSION-16 trial
entries.description: The COMPASSION-16 trial by Xiaohua Wu and colleagues addresses a crucial need in the management of advanced cervical cancer by evaluating cadonilimab, a novel bispecific antibody targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4, as a first-line therapy in combination with chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab. The COMPASSION-16 trial presents strong evidence supporting the efficacy of cadonilimab, with statistically significant improvements in progression-free survival and overall survival compared with standard chemotherapy.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Recommitting to global solidarity: introducing the Kigali Call to Action
entries.description: For more than two decades, the global community has united to fight the HIV pandemic, achieving remarkable progress. New HIV transmissions and AIDS-related deaths have dropped significantly, and millions of people are on life-saving treatment.1 The US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, UNAIDS, and The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria have been essential organisations in this response. Collectively, these institutions have invested in systems and strategies shaped by communities most affected by the disease.

Gender equity and women's roles are referenced and included under the broader equity narrative. entries.title: [Articles] Feasibility of interrupting the transmission of soil-transmitted helminths: the DeWorm3 community cluster-randomised controlled trial in Benin, India, and Malawi
entries.description: Soil-transmitted helminth transmission interruption might be possible in focal geographies but does not appear to be programmatically feasible within the evaluated timeframe. Community-wide MDA should be considered as an alternative strategy to school-based deworming programmes to improve equity and outcomes in helminth-endemic areas.

entries.title: [Perspectives] John Amuasi: calling for a socioecological approach to One Health
entries.description: John Amuasi is Head of the Global Health Department of the School of Public Health at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, Ghana, and Professor of Global One Health at the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, University of Eppendorf in Hamburg, Germany. With a career spanning more than 20 years, he is an accomplished global health researcher, working on infectious diseases, emerging pathogens, neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), and One Health. But, he says, his proudest research achievement is the report of the Lancet One Health Commission.

entries.title: [Comment] Balancing quality and quantity of life in older patients with breast cancer
entries.description: Overtreatment is considered harmful in terms of decreasing quality of life, wasting resources, and environmental damage.1–3 These risks are especially relevant when considering adjuvant chemotherapy besides adjuvant endocrine therapy for older adult patients (older than 70 years) with oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.4 Older patients with breast cancer represent around a third of all patients with breast cancer.4 However, patients older than 70 years with breast cancer, especially those with comorbidities, have generally been excluded from clinical trials.

entries.title: [World Report] 5 years on: the health legacy of the Beirut port blast
entries.description: The 2020 port explosion in Beirut killed more than 250 people and injured 7000. 5 years later, many Beirutis still suffer physical and mental ill effects. Clotilde Bigot reports from Lebanon.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Sudan's measles crisis and the global zero-dose gap
entries.description: When vaccines stop, measles returns. Since 2023, Sudan has witnessed several measles outbreaks, each a predictable outcome of systemic immunisation failure in a nation engulfed by civil war. Once a preventable disease, measles has re-emerged as a leading killer of children in conflict-affected regions of Sudan.

entries.description: The path to clinical expertise is complex and continues to evolve. New tools and technologies offer many opportunities but sharing stories and reflections continues to be an important aspect of building practice-based knowledge—cases discussed on ward rounds, dissected in breakrooms, and written up in the quiet moments between shifts or at the end of a long day. For many clinicians the first step towards publication and entry into academic medicine is not a trial report or a systematic review but documenting a case that puzzled, surprised, or moved them.

entries.title: [Correspondence] The invisible health crisis of Gaza's externally displaced
entries.description: Since the escalation of the conflict in Gaza in October, 2023, neighbouring countries have remained closed to Palestinian refugees, citing the long-term implications of any large-scale movement. Despite this reluctance to accept refugees, more than 115 000 Palestinians have managed to flee to Egypt.1 Although significant attention has been given to the conditions within Gaza, far less focus has been given to people displaced beyond its borders.

entries.description: The Lancet One Health Commission began its work in May, 2019,1 and in December of that year the COVID-19 pandemic emerged. entries.title: [The Lancet Commissions] The Lancet One Health Commission: harnessing our interconnectedness for equitable, sustainable, and healthy socioecological systems
entries.description: Industrialisation, urbanisation, and globalisation have substantially improved human life expectancy over the past century. In tandem, an expanding array of interlinked threats to humans, other animals, plants, and a myriad of other biotic and abiotic elements in our shared ecosystems has been generated. These threats include emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), non-communicable diseases (NCDs), jeopardised food safety and security, freshwater scarcity, climate change, pollution, and biodiversity loss.

entries.description: ADB has approved a loan of $350 million to support access to finance for women in Pakistan. entries.title: Scientists just recreated the Universe’s first molecule and solved a 13-billion-year-old puzzle
entries.description: Long before stars lit up the sky, the universe was a hot, dense place where simple chemistry quietly set the stage for everything to come. Scientists have now recreated the first molecule ever to form, helium hydride, and discovered it played a much bigger role in the birth of stars than we thought. Using a special ultra-cold lab setup, they mimicked conditions from over 13 billion years ago and found that this ancient molecule helped cool the universe just enough for stars to ignite. Their findings could rewrite part of the story about how the cosmos evolved from darkness to light.

entries.title: Ultra-hot Jupiter in death spiral may reveal how rocky worlds are born

entries.title: Astronomers detect life’s building blocks around a young star
entries.description: Astronomers using ALMA have discovered complex organic molecules, including potential precursors to life's building blocks, in the protoplanetary disc of a young star, V883 Orionis. This finding offers a tantalizing glimpse into how life-friendly chemistry may be far more widespread and inherited than previously thought.

entries.title: Ghost star’s planet orbits backward in a bizarre stellar system
entries.description: A bizarre planet defies cosmic norms: scientists have confirmed a giant planet orbiting in reverse around one star in a close binary system—an arrangement previously thought impossible. Using advanced tools, they discovered the companion star is a faint white dwarf that lost most of its mass billions of years ago. The team now believes this planet may be a rare second-generation world, born from or captured by the debris of its dying stellar neighbor. This find challenges traditional models of planet formation and opens a new chapter in exoplanetary science.

entries.title: AI just found 5 powerful materials that could replace lithium batteries

entries.title: What happens when light smashes into itself? Scientists just found out
entries.description: Physicists have discovered that when beams of light interact at the quantum level, they can generate ghost-like particles that briefly emerge from nothing and affect real matter. This rare phenomenon, known as light-on-light scattering, challenges the classical idea that light waves pass through each other untouched.

entries.title: Einstein was wrong: MIT just settled a 100-year quantum debate
entries.description: Physicists at MIT recreated the double-slit experiment using individual photons and atoms held in laser light, uncovering the true limits of light’s wave–particle duality. Their results proved Einstein’s proposal wrong and confirmed a core prediction of quantum mechanics.

entries.title: Scientists finally solve the mystery of what triggers lightning
entries.description: A Penn State-led research team has unraveled the long-standing mystery of how lightning begins inside thunderclouds. Their findings offer the first quantitative, physics-based explanation for lightning initiation—and a glimpse into the stormy heart of Earth’s atmosphere.

entries.title: Rutgers physicists just discovered a strange new state of matter
entries.description: At the edge of two exotic materials, scientists have discovered a new state of matter called a "quantum liquid crystal" that behaves unlike anything we've seen before. When a conductive Weyl semimetal and a magnetic spin ice meet under a powerful magnetic field, strange and exciting quantum behavior emerges—electrons flow in odd directions and break traditional symmetry. These findings could open doors to creating ultra-sensitive quantum sensors and exploring exotic states of matter in extreme environments.

entries.title: Pain relief without pills? VR nature scenes trigger the brain’s healing switch
entries.description: Stepping into a virtual forest or waterfall scene through VR could be the future of pain management. A new study shows that immersive virtual nature dramatically reduces pain sensitivity almost as effectively as medication. Researchers at the University of Exeter found that the more present participants felt in these 360-degree nature experiences, the stronger the pain-relieving effects. Brain scans confirmed that immersive VR scenes activated pain-modulating pathways, revealing that our brains can be coaxed into suppressing pain by simply feeling like we re in nature.

entries.title: Atomic-scale secrets: What really happens inside your battery
entries.description: Scientists have cracked open a mysterious layer inside batteries, using cutting-edge 3D atomic force microscopy to capture the dynamic molecular structures at their solid-liquid interfaces. These once-invisible electrical double layers (EDLs) twist, break, and reform in response to surface irregularities phenomena never seen before in real-world battery systems. The findings don t just refine our understanding of how batteries work at the microscopic level they could fundamentally change how we build and design next-generation energy storage.
